Since I'm active during the NY session I've been looking at the possibility of trading futures in addition to forex since things seem to go quiet in forex after the London close. I was looking back at the movements in crude and came across this setup. I decided to post it as a reminder that there are great trades to be had even when we miss the initial move out of HTF S/D.

With this setup we have a spike down into a fresh 4H demand zone. We then get a QM formation on the 1H and have a lengthy CP on the 15M which brings us to the 50% fib and an ignored demand zone.

Given the compression it would have been reasonable to set a limit at the top of the 1H ignored demand which also corresponds with a decision area on the 15M. Stop would be below the 1H demand which is also the QM area (about 35 pips). Expected return would be the top of the CP area which is 100 pips.

Often when I look at a chart and see that a big move has occurred I will say, Oh well, I missed that one and move on. I tend to focus too much on the LTF and this is a good reminder to keep the HTF in focus and look for the opportunity that comes as a result of that big move that I missed.

kruger wrote:

Josh wrote: My 2c - the move from the lows is not a false break -if you zoom in you should see where price reacted and why - it was not a typical false break IMO.

A false break involves big players using liquidity from novice traders (liquidity they know is present) to their advantage i.e. to offload their large orders.

This is of course very likely to happen at an already identified demand / supply zone (not always) - like the short setup in UCHF - i.e. from that DBD which is proven supply.

But there has to be a trap element otherwise it's not a false break and you don't get the order-flow that typically follows with a false break. For the trap element to be present we need to conclude that the area being broken is an area where novice traders are likely to have cluster of orders and I don't see that low as a big area relative to the high - but that's how I view false breaks - I look for obvious areas where novice traders will have clusters of orders and look to find a close supply / demand zone that can 'cause' the trap.

It often helps to visualise areas of price action bound between major decisions on value (S/D) This chart should speak volumes

Here are my trades and analysis from Tuesday. The trades are the numbers, and the letters refer to the analysis.

1 - Price rallies into HTF supply, forms a QM, so I went short. I think these are the easiest trades. Probably my favorite set up.

2 - Price falls into 15 min demand after moving down in a choppy and unconvincing fashion. I went long here for some more easy pips. 2 for 2 today.

A - Price stalls as it rallies into HFT supply, but breaks through to even higher supply. This level now flips from supply to demand.

B - As price falls, my first target was prior demand. I don't really care to trade demand levels that aren't drop based, but they certainly should be watched or used for targets.

C - Price goes back into demand zone from A. I was tempted to go long here, but as I said earlier, I don't really like demand levels like this.

D - After going long in trade 2, this supply zone was my first target. Unfortunately the remainder of my position was stopped at breakeven.

E - Price falls into hourly demand and forms a base. This was another tempting level, but the NY session was getting a little stale, and volatility was basically non-existent.

The W1 supply area was more than likely going to provoke some sort of reaction but when it came the reaction was rather meagre. The result was a consolidated range that lasted the best part of two days. Suffice to say that one day I hope to feel qualified enough to offer an explanation of why price consolidated here but for now I’ll proffer that it has something to do with profit taking and repositioning.

Experienced scalpers will have made some very nice trades in this zone. But the well-defined demand and supply levels shaded in white and the aggressive pin bar reaction to them ensured that I remained a market spectator for the first half of the week.

The first signs that pro money was preparing to move price came in the CP zone. The initial long tails indicate strong selling and after a further period of consolidation the break of support finally came at point 1.

Some of the more experienced AG traders sold into the break for the neat intraday target of local support, which I have annotated with the white dashed line. The more I observe these zones the more sense they make. Hopefully the more sense they make the more I’ll feel confident to trade them.

What I have referred to as Local Demand established local support and comes into play again to lift price to the origin of the break at 2. This move seems to serve two purposes:

1. Allows big money to test that the demand at the base of the large consolidated area has been absorbed.

2. Creates a fresh market of buyers along the way that big money can sell to.

After all the orders are filled at 2, supply exceeds demand and price falls. The long tails on the second and third red candle indicate the final grab of buyers to sell into before price falls off sharply.

Interesting here is the target for this phase of the move. The W1 RS zone confluences beautifully with a local demand level and closing profits for the short from 2 with an immediate reversal of position for the long at 3 formed the basis of If’s “No Brainer” trade, which he posted up shortly thereafter.

Things get even more interesting at 4. With the sustained period of selling (albeit weak) this is the first big money response that I can see to the institutional shakeout zone shaded blue and subsequent support area labelled Shakeout Support.

I think it’s important to add a note here. Until the shakeout support actually held I was not confident enough to take a trade from the area. I have deliberately presented a H1 chart here to illustrate the red high/low candle penultimate to the breakout. On my M30 chart this candle is actually coloured green. With what seemed to me like mixed signals I erred on the side of caution and sat out and watched.

While I was napping Doctor was buying the head (!!) of a reverse H/S. In retrospect I would have been happy to buy the right shoulder. The LTF charts exhibited all the right signals and it was my mistake to sit out. But as I keep on saying, one of the major benefits of doing one’s homework during the live market sessions seems to be that this stuff sticks.

The subsequent CP up climaxes in big money aggressively marking down price such that they are able to fill their last buy orders. Demand exceeds Supply and the resulting LQ is explosive.

Friday’s fun and games was a cakewalk for those guys who have reached the level of confidence in their trading to which students like me aspire. And so I close this homework by paying homage to Josh. What is it they say about imitation being the biggest form of flattery?

I have marked an area on the chart, which I call the Josh Trade. Apologies Josh if you ever get to read this but I first happened upon this type of very low risk high probability setup in your thread. I’ll leave it to you guys to search out the specifics of the trade suffice to say that Josh’s thread contains many examples that will point you in the right direction. Ironically, on Friday it was actually Kruger who bagged this one! Hats off to Kruger:)

Oedipus99 wrote: I'd love to get into this homework but I'm having real trouble figuring out what the difference between a bull/bear flag and compression looks like. If anyone wants to chime in I'd be grateful.

For the sake of understanding lets keep with an uptrend.

Compression price is moving up while at the same time spiking south taking out multiple demand zones at times. Olive triangle on chart. As a result when price heads south it just falls right through (usually).

Now a bull flag dips south to pickup more demand to continue north. As you can see on the chart. The dip south is often caused by a supply area to the left. Often times this makes a new demand area when price returns as you can also see on the chart. With compression demand is often used up throughout the whole compression zone.
